characters: Alidu: an inquisitive eight-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a sky-blue collared school shirt and khaki shorts.
Mariam: his bright eight-year-old Ghanaian friend wearing a neat white headscarf with a sky-blue-and-khaki school uniform dress.
Auntie Sherifa: a cheerful Ghanaian roadside vendor wearing a colourful gold-and-teal wrapper cloth and headwrap beside a blue insulated cooler box.
Their science teacher: a kind Ghanaian man wearing a crisp cream short-sleeved shirt and dark trousers.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious boy’s voice for Alidu; a bright girl’s voice for Mariam; a friendly seller’s voice for Auntie Sherifa
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and lively, with a pause at each change (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, cool tune with a drip-drip sound (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Frozen bags of drinking water are common on hot days in many Ghanaian towns and make a good, real example of a solid that melts.
The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the physical states of substances (B1.1.2.2, B2.1.2.2, B3.1.2.3).
Only drink water from a clean, safe source.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the explanation of solid, liquid and gas and the state changes match the NaCCA B2 and B3 standards.
Check that children are not told to drink water from unknown sources.

teacherGuide.overview: A frozen water bag that melts shows that water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas, and that heating and cooling change its state. Based on NaCCA Science content standards on physical states of substances.
learningGoals: Name the three states of matter.
Say what happens when ice is warmed.
Say how a solid, a liquid and a gas behave.
beforeReading: Hold up a bag of ice and ask: what will happen if we leave it here?
whileReading: Record the time and the changes every ten minutes.
afterReading: Put an ice cube on a plate in the sun and one in the shade and compare how fast they melt.
Draw ice, water and vapour in a line.
discussion: Why does ice melt in the sun?
Where does the water go if we leave it in the sun?
reflection: What other things melt when they are warmed?

support: Use a picture chain: ice, water, vapour.
stretch: Predict how long a bigger block will take to melt and test it.

culturalNotes: Frozen bags of drinking water are common on hot days in many Ghanaian towns and make a good, real example of a solid that melts.
The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the physical states of substances (B1.1.2.2, B2.1.2.2, B3.1.2.3).
Only drink water from a clean, safe source.
localiseThis: Use the frozen water bags or ice blocks that children know.
Never use hot water with children.
